documents.title: Code of Medical Ethics Informed Consent

chunks.content: Background Inguinal hernias account for approximately three-fourths of all abdominal wall hernias [ ]. Annually, about 300,000 repair of inguinal hernia surgeries are performed in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland [ ], 800,000 in the United States [ ], and 100,000 in the United Kingdom [ ]. These statistics demonstrate the increasing trend that has made repair of inguinal hernia one of the most common general surgical procedures, with an estimated global volume of 20 million cases per year [ , ]. Repair of inguinal hernia is primarily carried out using two surgical techniques: open surgery and laparoscopy [ , ]. However, both approaches present challenges in terms of postoperative pain management and complication control, which are ongoing concerns for physicians [ ]. Inadequate pain management has significant clinical implications, affecting surgical outcomes, patient satisfaction, and lead to undesirable physiological effects. These effects include cardiopulmonary complications, hypernatremia, sleep disturbances, delayed wound healing, prolonged hospitalization, and escalation of healthcare costs. Consequently, the effective management of acute postoperative pain assumes vital importance within the healthcare system [ ]. Nowadays, different drug protocols with various mechanisms effectively control acute postoperative pain. However, the side effects of analgesic drugs can cause sedation, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, respiratory depression, hypotension, and disturbances in the gastrointestinal and urinary systems [ ]. Therefore, non-pharmacological approaches for postoperative pain management have become more important [ ]. These approaches include therapeutic massage, transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) [ ], acupuncture, music therapy [ ], meditation, progressive muscle relaxation, and rhythmic breathing [ ]. Progressive muscle relaxation (PMR), first introduced by Jacobson, is a structured technique that involves regularly performing stretching and relaxation movements on major muscle groups, including the feet, chest, arms, and face. Furthermore, PMR is safe, cost-effective, easy to learn, and patients can easily perform it independently after surgery [ ]. Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of PMR in relieving pain in gastrointestinal surgeries [ ], arthroplasty [ ], mastectomy [ ], colonoscopy [ ], and lumbar disc herniation [ , ]. Rhythmic Breathing (RB) is an inherently gentle and harmonious technique that offers a non-invasive approach, capturing the patient’s attention. By skillfully diverting the mind from painful stimuli, RB utilizes the transformative power of distraction to facilitate the emergence of a profound sense of serenity that envelops the individual [ ]. There is a bidirectional relationship between pain and respiration. In clinical settings, it is generally recommended for patients experiencing pain to practice deep, slow breathing [ ]. Several studies in the literature have indicated that RB has a significant impact on pain relief. For instance, Marvi et al. found that RB is an effective technique for reducing pain caused by needle insertion in the fistula site of hemodialysis patients [ ]. Iyer et al. [ ] demonstrated that RB can effectively alleviate pain caused by burns. Moreover, Yuksel et al. discovered that respiratory exercises can significantly reduce the perception of labor pain, without side effects [ ]. Despite the efficacy of both PMR and RB techniques in reducing pain in patients, current research lacks a comparative study to determine the relative effectiveness of these two modalities in alleviating post-hernia surgery pain. Therefore, our objective was to investigate the effects of PMR and RB on pain after inguinal hernia surgery, considering the lack of sufficient evidence regarding their impact on post-hernia surgery pain control. The following three hypotheses were developed for this study: H1: RB positively affect the pain level of patients who have undergone surgery for Inguinal Hernia Repair. H2: PMR positively affect the pain level of patients who have undergone surgery for Inguinal Hernia Repair. H3: The pain level of patients undergoing Inguinal Hernia Repair who perform the PMR technique may similar to those who perform the RB. Methods Participants This parallel randomized controlled trial conducted over an 8 months period, From February 2023 to October 2023, at the Imam Hussain (AS) Hospital in Shahroud, a city located in northeastern Iran. The study population consisted of patients who had undergone open inguinal hernia surgery. The participants were divided into three groups: RB, PMR, and control with a 1:1:1 allocation ratio. The ethics committee of the Vice-Chancellor of Research approved the study at Shahroud University of Medical Sciences (Code: SHMU.REC.1401.186). It was registered on the Iranian Clinical trial Registry with identification number IRCT IRCT20200206046395N2 (registration date: 31/01/2023). The inclusion criteria for participation included the following factors: Undergoing surgery under general anesthesia. Postoperative consciousness. No addiction to drugs and narcotics. Ability to read and write in Persian. Absence of any motor and cognitive disorders. Age range of 18 to 75 years. No history of sedative and analgesic drug use for more than one month. The exclusion criteria included the following factors: Surgical complications such as infection and bleeding. Transfer to another medical center. Self-administration of analgesics by

Medical Sciences (Code: SHMU.REC.1401.186). It was registered on the Iranian Clinical trial Registry with identification number IRCT IRCT20200206046395N2 (registration date: 31/01/2023). The inclusion criteria for participation included the following factors: Undergoing surgery under general anesthesia. Postoperative consciousness. No addiction to drugs and narcotics. Ability to read and write in Persian. Absence of any motor and cognitive disorders. Age range of 18 to 75 years. No history of sedative and analgesic drug use for more than one month. The exclusion criteria included the following factors: Surgical complications such as infection and bleeding. Transfer to another medical center. Self-administration of analgesics by the patients. Sample size The sample size was calculated by using the mean and standard deviation of previous studies using PMR and RB techniques with Pain evaluation of patients [ , ]. Based on the formula for determining the ratio between two samples, with 95% confidence and 80% test power, the standard sample size for each group was calculated at 28 individuals (84 subjects in total). However, to the accuracy of the results, the sample size was increased to 40 participants per group, resulting in a total of 120 participants. n = Z 1 - α / 2 + Z 1 - β 2 σ 1 2 + σ 2 2 μ 1 - μ 2 2 Randomization and blinding After evaluating based on the inclusion and exclusion criteria and completing the informed consent form, the participants were included in the study and then assigned to three groups using a random block design. This was done by creating 20 blocks of six, with a computer program ensuring that the letters A, B, and C could be arranged together within each block. Each letter sequence was placed in an opaque envelop and placed in a respective box. During the registration process, envelopes were opened by a nurse who was trained in this area. Based on the opened envelope, participants were assigned to either the RB group (code A), PMR group (code B), or Control group (code C). In this study, participants were not blinded due to the nature of the intervention. Additionally, the statistical consultant and data collector were blinded regarding the random allocation. Outcomes The demographic and clinical profiles of the patients were gathered, including age, gender, habitat, job, history of previous surgeries, history of previous hospitalizations, anesthesia time, operation time, and Inguinal hernia side. This information was obtained through a researcher-designed questionnaire based on patients’ self-reports and documentation in their medical records. In this study, the primary outcome measure was pain, which was assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS). The VAS is a simple horizontal line ranging from 0 to 100 with equal intervals. It allows patients to rate their pain intensity in four categories: no pain, mild pain, moderate pain, and severe pain, corresponding to values of 0, 10–30, 40–70, and 80–100, respectively. Previous studies have established the validity and reliability of the VAS. Babamohammadi et al. reported a Cronbach’s alpha coefficient of 0.94 [ ], indicating strong internal consistency, and Alghadir et al. confirmed its internal reliability with a coefficient of 0.97 [ ]. Pain levels were measured at four time points: 3, 6, 12 and 24 h after surgery, both before and after each intervention, across all three groups. The secondary outcome measure was the amount of Pethidine analgesic administered within the first 24 h following surgery. Interventions On the evening before the surgical procedure, the researcher explained the objectives of this study to the patients after consulting with the surgical department authorities. Participants were then invited to take part in the study according to specific inclusion criteria. Afterwards, the researcher provided individual instruction on the PMR technique or RB technique using visual aids like posters, pamphlets, videos, and verbal guidance. It is important to note that the training continued until each participant was able to proficiently practice their assigned intervention technique multiple times, following the protocol under the researcher’s supervision. Group 1: RB The “Rhythmic Breathing” protocol consists of several distinct stages, that have been developed based on scientific literature [ , ]. This protocol involves four therapeutic sessions, scheduled at 3, 6, 12, and 24 h after surgery. Each session lasts for 20 min, and is administered under the close supervision of the researcher. Instructions for RB: Find a comfortable position on the bed. Close your eyes. Take a deep and slow inhalation through your nostrils for 3 s, holding the breath in your lungs. Exhale slowly through your mouth for 3 s, releasing the air from your lungs. Clear your mind of any tension and focus solely on the inhalation and exhalation of air. Repeat this process for 60 s. Take a 5-minute break and then repeat the cycle again [ , ]. Group 2: PMR The protocol for “Progressive Muscle Relaxation”

min, and is administered under the close supervision of the researcher. Instructions for RB: Find a comfortable position on the bed. Close your eyes. Take a deep and slow inhalation through your nostrils for 3 s, holding the breath in your lungs. Exhale slowly through your mouth for 3 s, releasing the air from your lungs. Clear your mind of any tension and focus solely on the inhalation and exhalation of air. Repeat this process for 60 s. Take a 5-minute break and then repeat the cycle again [ , ]. Group 2: PMR The protocol for “Progressive Muscle Relaxation” was developed based on relevant scientific literature [ ]. The implementation of this protocol consisted of four therapeutic sessions scheduled at specific time intervals: 3, 6, 12, and 24 h post-surgery. Each session lasted for 20 min and was conducted under the close supervision of the researcher. Instructions for PMR: Take a comfortable position on the bed. Concentrate on various muscle groups in a sequence: foot, leg, hip, chest, arm, shoulders, rear, and facial muscles. Contract each muscle group for 3 to 5 s, then fully relax for 10 to 15 s. Foot: Contract the muscles in your foot firmly and bring your toes together gently. Hold this position briefly before releasing the muscle tension. Leg: Activate the muscles in your calf and thigh simultaneously, pushing forward. Maintain this position briefly before relaxing the muscles. Hip: Concentrate on the muscles in your pelvis, buttocks, and lower back. Tighten these areas for a count of 5, then return to the initial position to induce relaxation. Chest: Direct your attention to the muscles in your chest. Inhale deeply and slowly for 3 to 5 s, then hold your breath, and release the tension in your chest muscles as you exhale fully. Arm: Focus on the muscles in your hands and arms. Contract these muscles while simultaneously pressing your forearms forward. Make a fist and maintain this position briefly before completely relaxing the muscles. Shoulder, Neck, and Back: Gently flex your shoulders, neck, and back. Hold the muscle tension for a few seconds, then release to achieve a state of relaxation. Facial: Elevate your eyebrows and create a furrow on your forehead. Contract your nose and cheeks. Press your lips together gently and hold for a few seconds, then gradually release [ ]. Group 3: Control Participants in this group received standard care including regular monitoring of vital signs such as heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and temperature to assess the patient’s general condition and detect any signs of complications. Additionally, they were administered prescribed analgesic medications. The researcher was present alongside the patients during the specified time intervals, instructing them to rest comfortably in a supine position. Furthermore, patients in all three groups received acetaminophen (Apotel) according to our standard organizational protocol to relieve postoperative pain. In cases of severe pain, an additional analgesic, Pethidine 25 mg/ml, was prescribed. Data analysis All statistical analyses were evaluated in SPSS version 25. A significance level of α < 0.05 was established. The normality of distribution for all data was confirmed by the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. The characteristics of the participants were analyzed using the chi-square test and analysis of variance. The analysis of variance test was used to compare the variable of pain before and after the intervention, as well as the amount of pethidine consumed in all three groups. Two-by-two comparisons of the groups were conducted through post hoc analysis using the Scheffe method. The effect of the intervention, time, and the interaction between group and time on the changes in pain intensity at 3, 6, 12, and 24 h after repair of hernia was evaluated using repeated-measures ANOVA. Results In the present study, all 120 patients were divided into three groups: RB, PMR, and control. All participants successfully completed the study (Fig. ). No significant differences were found between groups in demographic and clinical data at baseline assessment (Table ). There were no significant differences ( P > 0.05) in pain intensity between the RB and PMR groups at the indicated time points before the intervention (Table ; Fig. ). However, following the completion of the study, pain intensity decreased significantly in both experimental groups. The two-by-two comparison of groups in Table showed that the effect of PMR in reducing pain after the third intervention was significantly higher than that of the control group ( P < 0.05). However, there was no significant differences in the comparison of RB and control at this time ( P = 0.13). Additionally, there was no significant difference in the two-by-two comparison of PMR and RB interventions at 3, 6, 12, and 24 h after hernia repair ( P > 0.05). The analysis of variance with repeated measurements showed a significant difference between the groups in

both experimental groups. The two-by-two comparison of groups in Table showed that the effect of PMR in reducing pain after the third intervention was significantly higher than that of the control group ( P < 0.05). However, there was no significant differences in the comparison of RB and control at this time ( P = 0.13). Additionally, there was no significant difference in the two-by-two comparison of PMR and RB interventions at 3, 6, 12, and 24 h after hernia repair ( P > 0.05). The analysis of variance with repeated measurements showed a significant difference between the groups in mean pain after the intervention. Specifically, the pain intensity in the PMR ( P < 0.001) and RB ( P < 0.001) groups was significantly lower than in the control group. Additionally, the interventions reduced pain intensity over time ( P < 0.001) (Table ). Furthermore, the results of the analysis of variance showed that the pethidine consumption was significantly higher in the control group (23.12 ± 15.38), compared to the PMR (11.87 ± 14.96) and RB (10.62 ± 13.73) groups ( P < 0.001). Discussion In this RCT, we found that both RB and PMR reduced acute postoperative pain following open inguinal hernia repair surgery when added to routine postoperative care. Specifically, postoperative pain was reduced when participants in the intervention group received either RB or PMR compared to the control group. In addition, the present study demonstrates that the use of RB or PMR reduces the need for pethidine during 24 h after surgery. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to demonstrate the beneficial effects of RB on acute postoperative pain compared with PMR in patients after inguinal hernia repair. Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain the effectiveness of RB and PMR. The purpose of relaxation and breathing techniques is to reduce the activity of the sympathetic nervous system by inducing an opposite reaction to the stress response, namely a relaxation response. This response causes various physiological changes, including a decrease in heart rate, blood pressure, and levels of the stress hormones cortisol and adrenaline. Therefore, relaxation techniques may indirectly reduce pain perception by counteracting stress [ ]. Another possibility is that, according to the neuromatrix theory [ ], pain signals to the brain are inhibited by relaxation because RB and PMR reduce pain by stimulating pain-inhibitory processes in the brain. Furthermore, it has been shown that RB and PMR can effectively relieve pain by secreting endogenous opiates [ , ]. Earlier studies presented mixed results regarding the role of PMR and RB in pain relief and postoperative analgesia. Bahçeli and Karabulut [ ] found no benefit of PMR for pain relief on the first day after lumbar disc hernia surgery compared to the control group. In two clinical trials conducted by Pishgooie et al. [ ], and Babamohamadi et al. [ ], the results indicated that relaxation techniques, distraction, RB, and PMR did not have a significant impact on the consumption of analgesics after laminectomy and CABG surgeries. In our opinion, the difference in procedure and surgical techniques may play a role in this difference making it difficult to compare studies with our trial. Additionally, various social, economic, cultural, and clinical factors that significantly influence pain perception should be considered as important factors. Interestingly, in the literature, numerous clinical studies have confirmed that breathing exercises and relaxation techniques can positively contribute to pain relief [ – ]. Our results are consistent with the study by Aksu et al. [ ] which demonstrated that PMR significantly reduce pain in patients after thoracotomy surgery. Similarly, Hasanpour-Dehkordi et al. [ ], reported that PMR increases pain threshold, stress and anxiety tolerance, and adaptation level in surgical patients. Additionally, Loh et al. [ ] demonstrated the significant effect of PMR in relieving the pain of cancer patients who underwent major surgery. A systematic review and meta-analysis, presented evidence that breathing exercises are an effective method for reducing acute pain [ ]. Based on their research, Nasirnejad et al. [ ] demonstrated that rhythmic breathing significantly decreased the mean pain and anxiety scores in patients after CABG compared to the control group. Another study on patients undergoing laparoscopic surgery, evaluated the effect of breathing techniques on postoperative shoulder pain with results indicated a significant reduction in pain in the intervention group [ ]. Additionally, Sabherwal et al. [ ], and Ozhanli et al. [ ]. found similar results in reducing the amount of analgesic needed in respective trials. While these studies support our findings, it is important to note that the level of pain experienced by patients may vary depending on the type of surgery in each type of surgery. Ultimately, the findings of the present study support the theoretical foundations that the use of simple

undergoing laparoscopic surgery, evaluated the effect of breathing techniques on postoperative shoulder pain with results indicated a significant reduction in pain in the intervention group [ ]. Additionally, Sabherwal et al. [ ], and Ozhanli et al. [ ]. found similar results in reducing the amount of analgesic needed in respective trials. While these studies support our findings, it is important to note that the level of pain experienced by patients may vary depending on the type of surgery in each type of surgery. Ultimately, the findings of the present study support the theoretical foundations that the use of simple and non-invasive methods as non-pharmacological interventions can be beneficial in postoperative pain control. No adverse events related to PMR and RB occurred during the study period, making it relatively safe. In addition, it does not require additional costs, so efforts can be made to popularize it in future clinical practice. Study limitations Despite the strengths of the present study, it is important to note some limitations of our study. Firstly, the follow-up period for patients was limited because of short hospital stays and early discharges, which prevented us from examining the long-term effects of RB and PMR. Secondly, it is important to acknowledge the potential influence of ethnic and gender differences on pain perception, most of the patients in the present study were Iranian men. Therefore, the generalizability of our findings to other populations or demographic groups may be limited. Conducting further research involving diverse populations is essential to gain a comprehensive understanding of the impact of these factors on pain perception and the effectiveness of interventions. Conclusion The study found that RB and PMR were effective in reducing acute pain and decreasing pethidine consumption after Inguinal Hernia Repair. These findings have potential applications in various surgical fields, including inguinal hernia procedures, and can be used in training and clinical research. It is strongly recommended that healthcare team members, especially nurses, actively learn and teach RB and PMR. Implementing these approaches in patient care can effectively manage postoperative pain. Moreover, it is hoped that healthcare professionals will shift from traditional pain management methods to cost-effective complementary approaches for alleviating patients’ pain.

documents.title: Code of Medical Ethics Patient-Physician Relationship

chunks.content: Introduction Hysterectomy is the second most common operation performed on women after a cesarean Sect. [ ]. Over half a million women in the world undergo a hysterectomy procedure for reproductive issues each year [ ]. Most of hysterectomies are performed to treat benign conditions such as uterine fibroids, endometriosis, and symptoms such as uncomfortable menstrual bleeding [ ]. Some hysterectomies are performed inappropriately and are due to lack of diagnostic evaluation or failure of alternative treatments [ ]. The prevalence of peripartum hysterectomy among Iranian pregnant women was 2.81 per 1000 deliveries [ ]. Having a hysterectomy impacts a woman’s life in a significant manner. As such, deciding to undergo a hysterectomy is a difficult process for women, especially from a psychological perspective. Following a hysterectomy, women commonly experience changes in body perception, such as perceiving the body as different, feeling disabled, feeling hollow, believing they are different than other women and feeling that their body is attracting notice. The literature reports that women perceive themselves as different, alienated, impaired and changed after a hysterectomy and that they have difficulty making contact with the environment; furthermore, the more changes in body perception increase, the more depression increases [ ]. Not paying attention to the needs of women undergoing this process is not ethical. There are many effects from humankind relations around it. Therefore, a lot of ethical considerations should be undertaken about this common surgery. Ethical considerations in the clinical settings refer to a set of principles and values that “must be taken into account in order to prevent harm to others”. The 4 main ethical principles are beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy, and justice [ ]. Today, women’s autonomy in decisions related to hysterectomy, its completely private nature and keeping information confidential, considering women’s well-being and psychological satisfaction from care, justice in providing care and fair treatment regardless of socioeconomic status and protecting women regardless of their marital status, ethnicity, and religion is one of the things that should be considered [ ]. The majority of women experienced a positive attitude towards their decision to elect a hysterectomy based on their perceived sexual functioning and satisfaction; ideas of womanhood to include motherhood and femininity, and their trust in pre-surgical information from healthcare professionals, or other women [ ]. A meta-synthesis to identify and synthesize qualitative research evaluating the real feelings, inner needs and emotional experience of women undergoing hysterectomy found comprehensive consideration before hysterectomy, emotions and experience after hysterectomy, coping strategies such as seeking help from others [ ]. The World Health Organization has defined rights for patients, including the right to high-quality care and treatment, the right to fair access to health care and services, the right to access information, the right to confidentiality and privacy, and the right to informed consent including right to free will or independence of vote, the right to health education, the right to protest and complain, and the right to compensation [ ]. In addition, there are a lot of ethical consideration about hysterectomy as a choice for permanent sterilization [ ]. Medical staff, especially doctors and nurses, are required to protect the women’s rights and prevent them harm. These supports include informing and learning, honoring and respecting, supporting, protecting and ensuring continuity of care [ ]. Sometimes, clinical judgments based on the benefit and independence are incompatible. When there is no clear benefit and there are clear risks of hysterectomy, the woman, more than anyone else, is in a position to determine what treatment is best for her [ ]. Informed consent, as the most obvious manifestation of the moral principle of respect for individual autonomy, is one of the most important elements that must be observed before hysterectomy. The concept of informed consent is recognition of patients’ autonomy by health service providers and improvement of relationships with patients. One of the primary purposes of informed consent is to provide information about the treatment process or to improve individuals’ health care decisions. Informed consent can have the desired quality only when it reflects moral values [ ]. Patients have the right to make a decision about their treatment, and it is necessary to make such a decision by receiving complete information about the benefits and harms, alternative ways and possible costs [ ]. Medical staff should follow protocols and guidelines for informing about serious diseases such as uterus cancers. If she does not lose his spirit and can make positive decisions or if she has a fragile spirit and informing her will cause mental discomfort and delay in treatment, the patient’s condition should be informed to the family [ ]. Since ethics in medical centers are sometimes overshadowed by material issues, it is possible that it is not completely in line with the patient’s wishes. In many cases, surgeons and medical centers

If she does not lose his spirit and can make positive decisions or if she has a fragile spirit and informing her will cause mental discomfort and delay in treatment, the patient’s condition should be informed to the family [ ]. Since ethics in medical centers are sometimes overshadowed by material issues, it is possible that it is not completely in line with the patient’s wishes. In many cases, surgeons and medical centers are in conflict between ethical duties. The principles of medical ethics are beneficence (not doing harmful actions), not doing harm, and the right of the individual [ ]. There are very few studies on the intra-individual aspect of ethical considerations in hysterectomy. Although this issue is very important in medical ethics. The aspect of disclosing some diseases or surgeries in the common life, workplace, family and close friends has an important place in the field of medical ethics. Disclosure of this issue after marriage in Iran has created fewer challenges due to the necessity of the wife’s consent to surgery. However, there are illegal cases of surgery without the consent of the spouse or non-disclosure of the surgery before marriage [ ]. On the other hand, women’s privacy and confidentiality are very important in hysterectomy [ ]. Another issue sometimes happens in surgeries is under the table costs imposed on the patient. Determining the doctor’s salary is something that must be agreed upon by the parties, and when the doctor and the patient are satisfied with the set amount, the doctor is free to receive it, and basically, under the table does not make sense [ ]. Not only moral sensitivity of team of treatment but also support and moral considerations by close family, friends and society directly and indirectly affect on women’s sense towards loss of uterus. This society ranged from close family members, such as the husband, to the broad community cultures about how they see a woman without feminine organs [ ]. Husband’s support increase self-acceptance after hysterectomy [ ]. Some cultures support family (especially husband in fertility organ surgeries) involvement in management decisions. Even in these cultures, verifying patients’ preferences about the roles they wish their families to play is an ethical consideration [ ]. Women need visibility in the society as a whole person after their surgery. Even media as a powerful society arm influence on women’s decisions about hysterectomy. Some of them receive their informational support from the Internet, followed by family/friends, books/magazines, and other resources [ ]. Considering the importance of complying medical and general ethics and the lack of a study on determining ethical considerations in the communication network of women undergoing hysterectomy surgery, this study aimed to present these aspects in the patients’ lives by a standard researcher-made instrument. Method Research population married women who have been at least 2 months and at most 2 years since their hysterectomy. Research location Kerman city hospitals. This mixed method analysis (exploratory sequential mixed methods design was conducted in the whole of 2020 to create the “ethical considerations in communication network of women undergone hysterectomy” questionnaire and investigate its psychometric properties. Questionnaire development: The questionnaire was developed and tested using a mixed method approach in 3 phases. In the first phase, an item pool was created. Then, its validity was evaluated using Content Validity Ratio (CVR) and content validity index (CVI). In the third phase, Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) were conducted to assess its construct validity. To set up the initial item pool, 2 approaches were applied, a review of qualitative studies and existing literature, and individual interviews. To investigate the ethical considerations in communication network of women undergone hysterectomy, 10 participants were selected using purposeful sampling method and were interviewed using a semi-structured interview design. We create this tool according to the attitude of diverse women and then, measure its psychometric properties. The initial item pool consisted of 136 items related to different aspects of ethical considerations in communication network of women undergone hysterectomy. The items were scored on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 0 to 4 (from completely disagree to completely agree). The second phase involved an assessment of content validity using CVR and CVI. To determine the content validity ratio, 10 specialists working in the fields of midwifery, psychology, and reproductive health, nursing, medical education, medical ethic, and Islamic ethic accepted and completed the related forms. The CVR of each item was then calculated using the Lawshe formula. Since there were 10 evaluators in the present study, a minimum acceptable value of 0.62 was set for Lawshe. All items of the questionnaire had acceptable CVR (> 0.80). Moreover, all items

The CVR of each item was then calculated using the Lawshe formula. Since there were 10 evaluators in the present study, a minimum acceptable value of 0.62 was set for Lawshe. All items of the questionnaire had acceptable CVR (> 0.80). Moreover, all items had an acceptable CVI (0.70–0.79). In the third phase, construct validity and internal consistency were assessed. ranging from completely disagree to completely agree. The final questionnaire after creation, finalization and approval by experts in the field included 73 questions. Sampling This descriptive-cross-sectional research was conducted in 2020–2021 with the aim of investigating ethical considerations in the communication network of married women undergoing hysterectomy in selected hospitals in Kerman, after the approval of the code of ethics (ethic code: IR.KMU.REC.1399.067) from Kerman University of Medical Sciences. Then, in order to obtain the statistical population, all the hospitals in Kerman city where hysterectomy is performed will be included in the study. Four hospitals will be selected randomly among them. The entire research sample selected by whole population sampling based on the inclusion criteria. The researchers extracted the telephone numbers of the target women undergone hysterectomy and make a phone call. Those who are interested and qualified to participate in the study, and after obtaining informed consent, received a link of online questionnaire. Finally, 218 women were included in the final analysis. The response rate from telephone calls was 40%. Inclusion criteria The sample people must be at least two months old since their hysterectomy surgery, their age is less than 65 years old (elders not included), and a maximum of 2 years have passed since their hysterectomy and they are willing to cooperate and answer questions. Exclusion criteria Unwillingness to participate in the study. Data calculation and analysis method The questionnaire was analyzed by confirmatory factor analysis using Amos 24.0 software and using the maximum likelihood (ML) model. Questions with standardized coefficients less than 0.4 were removed. Cronbach’s alpha method was used to check the internal consistency of the questions. Ethical considerations Assuring the participants to keep the information confidential, necessary coordination with the deputy of the research centers and hospitals, full description of the research objectives and working methods to the officials of the centers and all the research units in written and oral form, respecting the research units and assuring them of the confidentiality of the information, obtaining oral consent from all participants and delivery of summary of results to respected hospital officials. Results Figure shows the investigated model of the instrument. Goodness of fit indices are reported in Table . The indices reported in Table are goodness of fit indices, each of which must be in a certain range to say that the model has a good fit. The range of changes of 𝛘2/df index is between 1 and 5. If the CFI index is higher than 0.9, it means that the model has a good fit. Another index that is used for the goodness of fit is PCFI, if its numerical value is greater than 0.6, it indicates the appropriate fit of the model. The next index that is examined is RMSE, and if it is between 0.05 and 0.10, we say that the model has a good fit. If the SRMR index is less than 0.1, the model has a good fit. If we pay attention to the numbers reported in the table above, we can see that only the CFI index is not within the acceptable range. In the Table , the path coefficients between the research variables are shown. For the reported paths, unstandardized and standardized coefficients, standard error, and critical ratio of the structural model are given. Standardized and unstandardized structural path coefficients, if they are significant, it means that the variables and their dimensions are significant and in the expected direction. All coefficients had a value above 0.4 and were significant (p-value < 0.001). In the Table , the descriptive information of the dimensions of the questionnaire was reported. The results of Cronbach’s alpha test showed that there is moderate to good internal consistency in all dimensions. Cronbach’s alpha for the whole questionnaire was calculated as 0.75, which shows that the internal consistency is at a good level. Discussion This study was designed to develop and conduct a questionnaire for the assessment of “ethical considerations in communication network of women undergone hysterectomy”. The psychometric properties of this tool including reliability (internal consistency) and factorial structure (CFA) were evaluated in a sample of women

Discussion This study was designed to develop and conduct a questionnaire for the assessment of “ethical considerations in communication network of women undergone hysterectomy”. The psychometric properties of this tool including reliability (internal consistency) and factorial structure (CFA) were evaluated in a sample of women undergone hysterectomy. Accordingly, the 8 factors extracted included “complying ethical consideration by the physician (a)”, “complying ethical consideration by medical team (b)”, “complying ethical consideration in the hospital (c)”, “complying ethical consideration by the secretory in the clinic (d)”, “complying ethical consideration by the spouse (e)”, and “complying ethical consideration by the family and friends (f)”, “complying ethical consideration by the media and society (g)” and “complying ethical consideration by herself (h)”. It is noteworthy that complying ethical considerations by a woman’s social network about this common surgery has influences on the attitude of women towards hysterectomy and its consequences. These issues point to the ethical issues that may happen around this surgery that affect on the individual thoughts and actions, marital and sexual adjustment and relationships as well as is affected by familial, social and cultural attitude towards hysterectomy [ , – ]. After hysterectomy, women not only feel a strong need for support from family members, especially their husbands, they are also seeking support from health care providers and their colleagues. Before the hysterectomy, it is recommended that family members be consulted to ensure the emotional support and care of women after the hysterectomy. It can help the adaptation to hysterectomy [ ]. Real experience of women after hysterectomy is related on comprehensive consideration before hysterectomy (a. disease factors; b. fertility factors; c. opinions of others); emotions and experience after hysterectomy (a. postoperative physical condition; b. psychological resilience to the loss of the uterus; c. changes in the couple’s relationship); coping strategies (a. self-denial and avoidance; b. change of perception and self‐adjustment; c. seek help from others) [ ]. In some low income societies, women faced with embedded social inequality in the form of gender biases, lack of labour security and a maternal-centric health system, demonstrated pragmatic agency in their decision to remove the uterus. When they experienced gynecological ailments, most sought two to three opinions and negotiated financial and logistical concerns. The health system offered few non-invasive services for non-maternal health issues. Moreover, women and health care providers believed there is limited utility of the uterus beyond childbearing. Women’s responsibilities as caretakers, workers and producers drove them to seek permanent solutions that would secure their long-term work and health security. Thus, hysterectomy emerged as a normalized treatment for gynecological ailments, particularly for low-income women with limited resources or awareness of potential side effects. In this setting, hysterectomy reflects the power structures and social inequalities in which women negotiated medical treatment and the need to reverse a culture of permanent solutions for low-income women [ ]. The majority of women experienced a positive attitude towards their decision to elect a hysterectomy based on their perceived sexual functioning and satisfaction; ideas of womanhood to include motherhood and femininity, and their trust in pre-surgical information from healthcare professionals, or other women [ ]. Educating couples on sexual affairs and rebuilding the self-image is related to offering enough information to the patients [ ]. Providing more information and education to them on the possible after-effects of hysterectomy and alternative options will enable them to make more informed choices [ ]. Performing non-therapeutic hysterectomy is subject to the clinical judgement of physicians according to their perception of the patient’s quality of life [ ]. The resources of information women depended on when making a decision to undergo hysterectomy varied and included a second opinion from another physician, social media, opinion from spouse/partner, second opinion from female family members, and opinion from friends [ ]. Information on regional rates and on the need for hysterectomy given through the mass media to the general population can change professional practices [ ]. For instance, YouTube is currently not an appropriate source for patients to gain information on hysterectomy. Physicians should be aware of the limitations and provide up-to-date and peer-reviewed content on the website [ ]. Establishing support groups to share the women’s experiences; and changing community views about hysterectomized women is a beneficial action towards them [ ]. Conclusion According to the results of this study, the reliability (internal consistency) and construct validity of the ethical considerations in the communication network of women undergoing hysterectomy questionnaire were confirmed. Conclusion According to the results of this study, the reliability (internal consistency) and construct validity of the ethical considerations in the communication network of women undergoing hysterectomy questionnaire were confirmed. However, in light of the study limitations, caution should be practiced in the interpretation of the results. There is a need for further longitudinal studies in multiple settings using random sampling methods. Limitations Response bias to provide socially desirable answers might be considered due to the inclusion of self-report questionnaires for data collection. Recommendations Future research can assess the validity of “ethical considerations in the communication network of women undergoing hysterectomy” questionnaire in cross-cultural environments that may have an impact on adoption. Future works are recommended to use a sample size large enough to examine measurement invariance of the questionnaire across aforementioned variables. This tool can be provided deeper insights of ethical considerations in the communication network of women undergoing hysterectomy to health providers.
